questions.statement: When my grandfather was a boy, he used to ________ to school every day. Now he takes the bus. Use "walk".
questions.context: A grandfather in Tunja describes how he travelled to school when he was a boy, compared with today.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Used to" is followed by the base form of the verb, so adding the past form "walked" breaks the structure.
Correct. After "used to" we always use the base form of the verb: used to + walk.
Incorrect. "Used to" is never followed by the "-ing" form; that belongs to "be used to walking".
Incorrect. The third person form belongs to the present simple, but "used to" describes a past habit.

questions.explanation:
"Used to" describes a habit or state that existed in the past and no longer does, and its grammar is completely regular: it is always followed by the base form of the verb. The contrast with "now he takes the bus" confirms that the past situation has changed.

questions.statement: Twenty years ago there were no buses on this road. Now they ________ every ten minutes. Use "come".
questions.context: A bus route on a road in Cali is described, comparing the past and the present service.

options.feedback: Correct. After "now" the present simple describes what happens at the present time, so the base form "come" is required.
Incorrect. "Came" is the past simple, which belongs to "twenty years ago" and not to the present situation.
Incorrect. "Used to come" describes a habit in the past, which is the opposite of what "now" introduces.
Incorrect. "Would come" describes a repeated action in the past, again not the current service.

questions.explanation:
The words "twenty years ago" and "now" fix the tense of each half of the sentence: the first half needs the past and the second half the present simple. Choosing the tense by the time expression is what keeps the contrast clear.

questions.statement: Which word means the place where people wait for the bus?
questions.context: A newcomer asks for information about the city bus system in Barranquilla.

options.feedback: Incorrect. A station is a large building used for trains or long-distance buses, not a place in the street.
Incorrect. A platform is the raised surface next to railway tracks where passengers wait for a train.
Correct. A "bus stop" is the place, usually in the street, where buses stop to pick up passengers.
Incorrect. A garage is a building where vehicles are repaired or kept, and passengers do not wait there.

questions.explanation:
City transport vocabulary needs precise words: "bus stop" for the place in the street, "station" for a large terminal, "platform" for the raised area beside railway tracks and "terminal" for the end of a bus line. Mixing them up makes descriptions of a city confusing.

questions.statement: Ten years ago the neighbourhood market was held in the square every Sunday. Now the organisers have moved it to the covered hall, because the square is used for the cycle race in the mornings and for outdoor films at night. Why did the organisers move the market?
questions.context: A short text about a neighbourhood market is used in a reading lesson about city spaces.

options.text: Because the square became too small.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Nothing in the text says the square is too small; the reason given is the other activities that take place there.

options.text: Because people stopped going to the market.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The text does not report a fall in attendance at the market at any point.

options.text: Because the square is now used for other activities.
options.feedback: Correct. The text explains that the square is now taken by the cycle race in the morning and by outdoor films at night.

options.text: Because the covered hall is cheaper to rent.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The cost of the hall is never mentioned in the passage, so that reason is invented.

questions.explanation:
The text gives the reason with the word "because", and it names two specific activities that now occupy the square. A reading answer that repeats the stated cause is correct; one that invents a cause, such as the size of the space or the price, has no support in the passage.

questions.statement: I ________ living in a small flat near the river, so I am not used to the noise of the traffic.
questions.context: A student explains why she has adapted to her new neighbourhood in Bogotá.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Used to living" describes a habit in the past, but the sentence is about a present state and a present reaction.
Incorrect. "Was used to" is the past of being accustomed; the sentence needs the present form "am used to".
Incorrect. "Used to" is never followed by "being"; the structure that requires "-ing" is "be used to being".
Correct. "Am used to" means being accustomed to something, which is exactly what the contrast with "not used to the noise" describes.

questions.explanation:
Two similar structures must be separated: "used to do" refers to a past habit, while "be used to doing" refers to being accustomed to something in the present. The second part of the sentence, "so I am not used to the noise", is the clue that this is a matter of being accustomed.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Cycling through the city is ________ than driving, because you do not have to look for a place to park.
questions.context: Two commuters discuss why they prefer different ways of moving through the city.

options.feedback: Incorrect. The base form "healthy" cannot be compared with "than"; a comparative form is required.
Incorrect. "Healthiest" is the superlative and needs "the" plus a group, never the word "than".
Incorrect. For short adjectives we add "-ier", so we say "healthier" and not "more healthy".
Correct. Short adjectives take "-ier" to form the comparative, so healthy becomes healthier, and it is followed by "than".

questions.explanation:
Adjectives of one syllable form the comparative by adding "-er" or "-ier", while longer adjectives use "more". The superlative uses "-est" or "most" and requires "the". Comparing forms correctly is what makes the sentence grammatically complete with "than".

questions.statement: The city council has asked residents to send comments on the new tram line. So far the strongest objection is that the line will pass in front of houses and the construction noise will last nine months. The council says the works will be done at night. What does the council do with the noise problem?
questions.context: A news report describes a public consultation about a new tram line in a Colombian city.

options.text: It plans to do the noisy works at night.
options.feedback: Correct. The text says the council will carry out the works at night, which directly addresses the noise objection.

options.text: It has cancelled the tram line.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The line is still being discussed and no cancellation is mentioned anywhere in the report.

options.text: It has promised to shorten the line.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Nothing in the text says that the length of the line will change.

options.text: It has ignored the residents' objections.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The council asked for comments and answered them, so it did not simply ignore the residents.

questions.explanation:
A question about what an institution "does" must be answered with the action reported in the text. Doing the works at night is a direct response to the noise complaint, while cancelling the line, shortening it or ignoring the objections are actions the report never mentions.

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence about urban transport.
questions.context: A writing exercise focuses on the articles and prepositions used to talk about transport.

options.text: "I go to work by the TransMilenio every day."
options.feedback: Incorrect. Proper names of specific services take no article, so it must be "by TransMilenio" without "the".
Incorrect. The verb "travel" needs a preposition such as "by" or "on" before the means of transport.

options.text: "I travel on public transport to avoid traffic."
options.feedback: Correct. "Travel on" is the natural collocation, and "public transport" used in a general sense takes no article.

options.text: "I go home by the bus every morning, and it is always full."
options.feedback: Incorrect. In the general sense the noun takes no article: "by bus"; "by the bus" would refer to one specific vehicle.

questions.explanation:
Two rules govern articles with transport: proper names of services and general uses of the noun "bus" take no article, and the verbs of movement are followed by "by" or "on". Applying both rules removes the article error and the missing preposition in the same step.

questions.statement: If the city built more cycle lanes, fewer people ________ drive, and the air would be cleaner.
questions.context: A proposal about city infrastructure argues for change in the way people travel.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Fewer people would drive" says the opposite of what the sentence intends, which is that fewer people would drive.
Correct. In the second conditional the result clause uses "would not" plus the base form of the verb.
Incorrect. "Will not" belongs to the first conditional, which talks about real future possibilities.
Incorrect. The past simple "did not" does not match the structure "if ... , would ...", which is entirely in the present.

questions.explanation:
The second conditional describes an unreal or probable situation: "if" + present simple in the condition and "would" + base form in the result. The negative of the result is simply "would not", while "will not" and "did not" belong to other conditional forms.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: My neighbourhood ________ have a small market on the corner; now there is a large supermarket two streets away. Use "used to".
questions.context: A student compares a neighbourhood of ten years ago with the neighbourhood today.

options.feedback: Correct. "Used to have" describes a situation that existed in the past and no longer does, which is the contrast the sentence makes.
Incorrect. "Was used to" means being accustomed to, and it would need a noun or an "-ing" form after it.
Incorrect. "Would have" describes a hypothetical past, not a real former situation that definitely existed.
Incorrect. "Used have" omits the "to" that must follow "used", so the structure is incomplete.

questions.explanation:
"Used to" has exactly two parts: the phrase "used to" plus the base form of the verb. It describes real past states, and it is followed by a contrast such as "now there is", which marks the change. "Was used to" expresses a different idea altogether: being accustomed.

questions.statement: Between 2015 and 2024 the average time that residents of the city spent travelling to work fell from seventy-two minutes to fifty-one minutes. During the same period the network of buses was extended and a new cycle lane was built along the main avenue. What can be inferred about the city?
questions.context: A statistics report measures how long citizens of a city take to reach work.

options.text: Residents began to work fewer hours.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The text does not mention working hours at all, so that cannot be inferred.

options.text: The city built a new railway.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only buses and a cycle lane are mentioned; no railway appears in the report.
Correct. The travel time fell by twenty-one minutes, which directly shows that the average journey became shorter.
Incorrect. No information about prices is given, so this conclusion has no basis.

questions.explanation:
The only inference supported by the data is the one about duration: from seventy-two to fifty-one minutes means a shorter average journey. Explanations about hours worked, railways or prices introduce new subjects that the report never mentions, so they are not valid inferences.

questions.statement: A friend asks you how to get from their house to the university, which is twenty minutes away by bus. Which reply is the most useful?
questions.context: A new student asks a housemate how to reach the university from the neighbourhood.

options.text: "Take the bus, walk five minutes to the stop, and get off two stops before the main gate."
options.feedback: Correct. It gives concrete, ordered instructions that cover the walk, the ride and the exact place to get off.
Incorrect. "You'll find it" gives no information about the route, so it cannot help anyone travel.

options.text: "The bus is always full, but nobody ever waits more than five minutes."
options.feedback: Incorrect. It describes the general situation without saying what to do, so it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: "You should not travel by bus; buses do not exist."
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Buses do not exist" is obviously false and ignores the friend's real question.

questions.explanation:
A useful answer to a practical question contains the actions the person must carry out, in order. Option A gives three of them. Describing the situation without instructing, or giving information that is not true, leaves the listener without a plan to follow.
